links.note: The false option is 'rational numbers are NOT closed under addition'; spotting it needs the fact that the sum of two rationals is always rational, which is this concept exactly.
The false option is that natural numbers are closed under subtraction. What decides it is the which-set-is-closed-under-which-operation comparison, not the rationals-specific statement of 31259.
True option: naturals are closed under multiplication, the other three denying closure for wholes, integers and rationals. Again the closure table across number sets.
True option: whole numbers are not closed under division - word for word one half of this concept's statement about whole numbers.
0 is not a natural number but is a whole number, an integer and a rational. That zero sits outside the naturals and was added to make the whole numbers is precisely this concept.
1/2 is a rational number and none of the other three kinds; the test applied is the p/q definition of a rational number.
a + b = b + a named as the commutative law of addition - the order-does-not-matter-for-addition statement.

a x b = b x a, commutativity for MULTIPLICATION. The set has no multiplication-specific commutativity concept; 31264 is the one that has commutativity checked operation by operation rather than only for addition, so it and not 31261 is the home.
(a+b)+c = a+(b+c) named as the associative law for addition - grouping either way gives the same sum.
a(b+c) = ab+ac named as the distributive law, which is this concept's rule verbatim.
The untrue statement is 2/3 - 5/4 = 5/4 - 2/3: one worked counterexample showing subtraction is not commutative, while the addition and multiplication options are true.
Names the set of numbers expressible as p/q with p, q integers and q non-zero - the definition of a rational number stated back.
Names the property behind 'the sum of any two rationals is always rational' as closure. The statement to be named is this concept's own sentence.
